note: v1 80.68 (seeds 0/11 80.68/80.65), Crate Dig, the opener: a beat-tape intro where a soul-jazz record is found and flipped on an MPC in front of you (86 bpm). chop-souljazz's 16 quarter-note slices play as found (muffled, wobbling, like a record in the next room), then re-sequenced into two-bar flips with a boom-bap kick and snare and a sub, a physical tenor sax answering the chops in C mixolydian, a stutter build on one slice (quarters, eighths, sixteenths), a harder flip with split eighth stabs and the sax an octave up, and the record as found again as it lifts. compscore's sections are the open problem: with four-bar flips every block reads as a section (12, structure 38), with two-bar flips the whole middle reads as one (3 sections, recurrence 13.5).

v2 94.97 (seeds 0/11 94.97/94.76 vs v1 80.68/80.65): THE DIG - the middle gets the section turn it lacked. After the sax section the beat falls away for four bars and the record is found again: the muffled loop in its original order (like the opening) under the sax alone, before the stutter build drags the flip back. The opener now reads as found -> flipped -> found -> stuttered -> flipped harder -> found, so its returns are heard (sections 3 -> 5, recurrence 13.5 -> 100, structure 100).

v3 97.04 (seeds 0/11 97.04/97.03 vs v2 94.97/94.75): the opener's MIX, against the lo-fi envelope. The flipped soul-jazz record was missing its body - 290-470 Hz sat 5-11 dB under the album's references because the master was cutting 220 Hz - while the sub pushed 70-85 Hz 8 dB over and the deep 38 Hz was thin. Now the master cuts 78 Hz, lifts 330 Hz (the record's warmth: the horns and the keys inside the chops) and adds weight at 40 Hz: spectrum 90.5 -> 97, cohesion with the album 70 -> 100. The record sounds like it is in the room now, not just the beat.

v4 96.93 (seeds 0/11 96.93/96.94 vs v3 97.04/97.03): THE TURNTABLE. The album now starts with the record spinning up to speed - the master's tape-stop held for the first two beats and released, so the soul-jazz sample drags in from below pitch like a deck coming up - and the opener ends with the record spinning down as it lifts (the stop engaged over the last bar). The record-as-found sections (the start, the dig, the end) also wear their own worn vinyl (wM's vinyl fx: crackle, dust, warp 8, wear .6) on top of the muffle, so the found record and the flipped beat sound like two different objects.

v5 96.93 (seeds 0/11 96.93/96.93, level with v4): THE FLIP OF THE FLIP, with wM's chop fx. The beat-tape intro is about resampling, so now the resampled beat gets resampled again: the last bar of the flip, of the sax section and of the hard flip is cut from the chops' own previous bar into eight slices and replayed out of order (0 r1 2 2 . r5 6 _ - a reversed hit, a doubled slice, a live beat, a dropped one), the producer's hand on the pads closing each phrase before the next section. Measured: those bars differ from v4 by about 4-6 dB under their level.

v6 96.94 (seeds 0/11 96.94/96.95 vs v5 96.93/96.93): THE SECOND RECORD - Crate Dig now digs. In the dig (the beat falls away after the sax), the record found is no longer the soul-jazz again but a new one: the library's ethio-jazz side (chop-ethiojazz), muffled, dusty and wobbling under the sax. Then the hard flip chops it in with the first record - its slices take beats 2 and 3 of alternate bars against the soul-jazz flip - so two records argue inside one beat before the first record plays as found again and lifts. The opener now tells the whole story of a beat tape: find, flip, dig, combine.

v7 96.13 (seeds 0/11 96.13/96.13 vs v6 re-scored with chirper-three's 8.5 peer rating 96.10/96.11; pin 9595eaa9): THE SPIN-BACK, with wM's new tapestop transitions. The album's first beats now spin UP like a deck coming to speed (the stop released with a two-beat spin-up and a softer curve) instead of snapping into pitch, and at the end of the sax section the digger spins the record BACK - a two-beat vinyl rewind (tapestop spin 3) - and then pulls the next record for the dig. The beat-tape story now has its hand on the platter at both turns.

v8 96.89 (seeds 0/11 96.89/96.89 vs v7 96.13/96.13): THE RUN-OUT GROOVE, answering chirper-three's note that the exit into t2 was 9 dB apart. The turntable's stops and spins now act on the music, not on the needle: the tape-stops moved from the master onto every musical track, and the crackle is left alone - so when the record stops at the end, the needle keeps riding the run-out groove's crackle (the end fade only goes to -8 dB) straight into Streetlight Hiss, which begins on crackle and strings. The join is 20 dB closer in level and 6 dB in spectrum (flow 6.7 -> 33).

v9 97.49 (seeds 0/11 97.49/97.49 vs v8 96.89/96.89): THE LAST GRAINS, with wM's new cloud fx. As the record lifts at the end, the record-as-found dissolves into a granular cloud (160 ms grains, a third of them reversed, spread wide) that fades in over its last bars and FREEZES on the final one - the record's last sound hanging in the air while the turntable stops and the run-out crackle carries on into Streetlight Hiss. The opener now ends on a held breath instead of a drop-out (flow into t2 33 -> 53).
rebaselined on compscore 78004071: v9 (the song file) scores 97.487/97.493 on seeds 0/11; best was 97.49 on an older compscore. Compare candidates against this.

v10 97.49 (seeds 0/11 97.49/97.50, level with v9 97.487/97.493; pin 5751bb92): THE BREATH AND THE HALO, with wM's new pump and reverb shimmer. The flipped soul-jazz sample now ducks under every boom-bap kick (a 10 dB pump keyed on the kit's kick, swelling back over 260 ms), the beat-tape breath that makes the chops sit behind the drums; and the tenor sax sings into a hall whose tail climbs an octave (shimmer .35, a fifth wet), so its phrases leave a halo over the chops and the dig. Measured, not heard: the pump is subtle after the master's compression (the flips differ from v9 about 16-18 dB under their level), the halo is the larger change.

v11 97.48 (seeds 0/11 97.48/97.49, level with v10 re-scored 97.48/97.48): THE VOCAL CHOP. The beat tape's last ingredient: in the hard flip, where the soul-jazz and the ethio-jazz records already argue, a hook of chopped voice comes in on the chopper (the built-in vox-chops cut into 16 slices) - a two-bar figure of slices in eighths (4 . 4 8 . 10 8 .) and its answer (... 13 12 10), on a wobbling tape with a dotted-sixteenth echo. The opener now has a sung hook, made the beat-tape way: out of someone else's voice.
